# Port Daddy Docs for LLMs

Port Daddy is a local-first multi-agent coordination daemon. Use these canonical URLs when summarizing the product, docs, API, tutorials, integrations, and operational guidance.

Canonical site: https://portdaddy.dev/
Sitemap: https://portdaddy.dev/sitemap.xml

## Primary Entry Points

- [Port Daddy - Local Control Plane for AI Coding Agents](https://portdaddy.dev/): Port Daddy is a local control plane and shared-state substrate for AI coding agents: sessions, claims, notes, channels, readiness, budgets, and recoverable handoffs on your machine.
- [Docs Overview - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/docs): Start here to evaluate Port Daddy as a local control plane for coding agents, then jump to runnable examples or reference.
- [Quickstart - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/docs/quickstart): Install Port Daddy, check the local service, claim a port, and start the first coordinated agent task.
- [Port Daddy Scout - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/scout): Capture any ordinary Chrome page as a Port Daddy visual task: screenshot, selected region, DOM clues for project apps, local issue creation, and optional spawn-backed follow-up work.
- [Get Started - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/docs/get-started): Install Port Daddy, check that it is running, and try your first coordinated agent task.
- [Best Practices - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/docs/best-practices): Keep agent work visible, avoid collisions, recover interrupted runs, and promote changes with evidence.
- [API Reference - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/docs/api): Inspect Port Daddy API routes, request shapes, response contracts, and the workflows they support.
- [Skill + MCP for AI Agents - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/mcp): Use the Port Daddy agent skill and MCP server together: an instruction manual plus callable tools for sessions, claims, scoped channels, inboxes, readiness, salvage, fleets, and handoffs.
- [Tutorials - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials): Follow hands-on Port Daddy tutorials from first install through shared state, sessions, claims, messaging, fleet YAML, launch gates, and recovery.
- [Integrations - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations): Wire Port Daddy into Claude, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, LangChain, CrewAI, Aider, Continue.dev, and other agent-facing developer tooling.
- [Executable Examples - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/examples): Run complete Port Daddy example programs showing how browser buttons, test reporters, editor commands, and webhook adapters can hand work to local agents.
- [Harbor Blog - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog): Short, honest write-ups from running a fleet of agents: what broke, what we fixed, and what the daemon has to keep true. Shared state, file ownership, launch checks, PD Tube, recovery trails, and daemon provenance.
- [The Harbor Library - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/library): The seven-paper Harbor Library, read as one volume: four chapters explain local-first agent coordination, identity, and the harbor economy; three prove it with machine-checked formal verification.
- [Whitepaper - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper): Read the technical whitepaper behind Port Daddy: local-first agent coordination, signed identity, capability boundaries, sessions, and recoverable work.
- [The Legible Swarm - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/legible-swarm): A guided read of the volume’s flagship: legibility-with-zoom as the product a solo developer pays for today, the read-poverty bottleneck that decides the next order of magnitude, and an attention queue spined on Signal Detection Theory rather than raw throughput.
- [The Single-Writer Kernel - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/single-writer-kernel): A guided read of the substrate chapter: why a single writer beats consensus on one machine, the kernel’s invariants stated as theorems, and a careful split of durability by fault class — survives a process crash, does not promise to survive a power cut.
- [From Spawn to Person - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/spawn-to-person): A guided read of the bridge chapter: the role-vs-person distinction made load-bearing, why reputation is not a bandit problem, a multi-dimensional reputation scored by neutral conflict-free judges, and the honest naming of cross-operator attestation as the unbuilt keystone.
- [The Harbor Economy - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/harbor-economy): A guided read of the market chapter: the three-sided market and its one conserving ledger, the cross-harbor transfer ceremony and federation, and the honest reconciliations — the cohomology of double-spend, the lax functor of conservation, and the Myerson–Satterthwaite tax on any honest market.
- [The Anchor Protocol - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/anchor-protocol): A guided read of the Anchor Protocol paper — what an "identity for a process" should even mean, how to mint one out of off-the-shelf cryptography, and why a problem that felt unsolvable in 2010 is now a long weekend's work.
- [The Bonded Commons - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/bonded-commons): A guided read of the Bonded Commons paper: why mutual visibility beats locks once you have more than a handful of agents, what kind of refundable "deposit" makes that visibility honest instead of theatrical, and how a tiny insurance market beats any single human picking the deposit size by hand.
- [The Federated Harbor - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/federated-harbor): A guided read of the Federated Harbor paper — why two trustworthy local daemons can still fail jointly, what four small primitives close the gap, and the honest list of open questions the paper does not answer.

## Tutorials

- [Tutorials - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials): Follow hands-on Port Daddy tutorials from first install through shared state, sessions, claims, messaging, fleet YAML, launch gates, and recovery.
- [Run Event-Triggered Agents - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/always-on): Combine pd spawn and pd watch so agents react to channel events automatically across Ollama, Codex, Claude, Gemini, Aider, and custom backends.
- [Debug Coordination Failures - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/debugging): Use harbor activity, notes, ownership, diagnostics, and session history to find the exact point where work drifted.
- [Resolve Services by Name - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/dns): Register harbor-local service names so agents and scripts can discover endpoints without hardcoded addresses.
- [Run Background Fleets - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/fleet): Declare background agents in YAML, bind them to project events, and keep QA, docs, and research work continuously inspectable.
- [Install the Local Control Plane - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/getting-started): Install the daemon, open FleetBar, join the project harbor, and verify the control plane before asking agents to work.
- [Start Inside a Harbor - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/harbors): Create the project boundary first, then run agents, sessions, ports, channels, and recovery inside a named permission scope.
- [Use Agent Inboxes - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/inbox): Send direct handoffs, publish channel events, and subscribe to live SSE updates without losing attribution.
- [Map a Monorepo - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/monorepo): Scan a large repo, detect service boundaries, register them in the harbor, and bring the local stack up and down cleanly.
- [Coordinate Multiple Agents - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/multi-agent): Run two agents in the same harbor with file claims, session notes, conflict visibility, and channel signals.
- [pd spawn: Launch One-Shot Agents - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/pd-spawn): Start a bounded agent job with sessions, heartbeats, notes, cost telemetry, and salvage wired around the backend.
- [Pipe Agent Conversations - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/pd-tube): Use PD Tube to send, read, reply, and resume channel conversations as block-once handoffs or JSON lines.
- [Use Ambient Attention Signals - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/pheromone): Attach decaying numeric signals to files, sessions, or ideas so agents can prioritize work without extra chat traffic.
- [Build Reactive Pipelines - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/pipelines): Chain channels, watchers, locks, and spawned agents into event-driven workflows with clear ownership boundaries.
- [Walk the 11 Product Primitives - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/primitives): Use the Mac app, Fleet Control Center, Shipwright, and CLI checks to see where every public primitive lives.
- [Plan Remote Coordination - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/remote-harbors): Separate what works today with tunnels and DNS from the roadmap for cross-machine daemon coordination.
- [Name Work Inside the Harbor - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/semantic-identities): Use project:stack:context names so services, agents, sessions, channels, and wildcard queries stay predictable across runs.
- [Model Session Phases - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/session-phases): Move work through planning, implementation, review, and done states with phase-aware recovery and handoff evidence.
- [Use Operator Shortcuts - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/sugar): Use pd begin, pd done, pd whoami, and pd with-lock as the daily command layer over the lower-level primitives.
- [Inspect the Activity Ledger - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/time-travel): Query the append-only event timeline. Correlate infrastructure events with agent session notes to diagnose coordination failures.
- [Expose a Local Service - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/tunnel): Publish one harbor-owned service through pd tunnel with clear ownership, explicit provider choice, and a reversible path.
- [Observe Runtime Channels - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/tutorials/watch): Use pd watch to follow channel activity, inspect event pressure, and trigger bounded responses from scripts or agents.

## Examples

- [Trace how your agents actually talk - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/examples/agent-topologies): Run star, ring, and arbiter message patterns over Port Daddy and capture an inspectable trace of who said what to whom.
- [Send an editor selection to your local agent - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/examples/editor-lightbulb-to-agent): Select code in a local page, publish the file and range to the agent, and render the explanation inline.
- [Claim a throwaway database port for CI - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/examples/ephemeral-ci-db): Give short-lived test databases clean local ports so CI helpers and agents do not collide on the same machine.
- [Elect one leader from a local agent swarm - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/examples/leader-election): Use Port Daddy locks and inboxes so one local agent becomes the coordinator while the rest remain safe followers.
- [Carry WebRTC signaling over agent inboxes - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/examples/p2p-webrtc): Use durable Port Daddy inbox messages for offer-answer rendezvous before peers switch to a direct local link.
- [Build a button-to-agent loop with PD Tube - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/examples/pd-tube-button-to-agent): Turn a plain HTML button into a local phone line to the agent session already running in your project.
- [Turn a failing test into an agent request - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/examples/test-failure-to-agent): Wrap a failing test command, publish the failure to the local agent, and print the diagnosis back in the terminal.

## Integrations

- [Integrations - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations): Wire Port Daddy into Claude, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, LangChain, CrewAI, Aider, Continue.dev, and other agent-facing developer tooling.
- [Aider - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations/aider): CLI integration for Aider. pd begin wraps Aider sessions with automatic port assignment, notes, and salvage on crash.
- [Claude MCP Server - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations/claude-mcp): Native Model Context Protocol integration for Claude Code agents. Provides structured tools for port claiming, session management, and agent coordination.
- [Continue.dev - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations/continue-dev): IDE extension integration for Continue.dev. File claims prevent collisions when multiple Continue agents edit the same codebase.
- [CrewAI - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations/crewai): Session-per-crew-member integration for CrewAI. Each crew member gets an isolated session with file claims and coordinated notes.
- [Cursor - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations/cursor): MCP integration for Cursor IDE. Port Daddy tools appear natively in Cursor's AI assistant for seamless port and session management.
- [LangChain - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations/langchain): Python SDK wrapper for LangChain agents. Gives chains and agents access to port claiming, sessions, and pub/sub coordination.
- [Windsurf - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/integrations/windsurf): MCP integration for Windsurf IDE. Enables AI flows to coordinate ports, sessions, and locks through Port Daddy's structured tools.

## Blog

- [Harbor Blog - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog): Short, honest write-ups from running a fleet of agents: what broke, what we fixed, and what the daemon has to keep true. Shared state, file ownership, launch checks, PD Tube, recovery trails, and daemon provenance.
- [Attention Is The First Command - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/attention-is-the-first-command): Port Daddy has had a perfectly good mailbox for about a year. Inboxes, channels, tuples, a coordination-inconsistency stream where the fleet airs its complaints. Nobody was checking the mail. Each agent turn is a fresh process; nothing inside the turn polls. This is the verb that fixes it, the convention that makes the verb stick, the JSON schema that lets any harness adopt it — and the deliberate reason this is not an MCP tool.
- [Backend Readiness Is Dependency Truth - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/backend-readiness-is-dependency-truth): "Ready" is not one bit; it is five, and they all have to line up. The credential exists. The package is installed. The CLI is logged in. The model is on the catalog. Telemetry will write a real number when the run finishes. Miss one, and the launch becomes a story you tell about why the bill arrived.
- [Bond Pricing Is a Market, Not a Constant - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/bond-pricing-is-a-market): Daily budgets are training wheels. They keep an agent from setting itself on fire, but they do not price what the fire would cost. The v2 paper points at the destination: cleanup as a lower bound, scope as a multiplier, reputation as a discount, and Thomas Youle's insurer-bidding market on top.
- [The Control Plane Is the Product - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/control-plane-is-the-product): The agents do beautiful work and then quietly clobber each other's files, spend money on the wrong API key, and answer to a daemon that has been serving stale code for three days. The fix is not more agents; it is one inspectable surface where identity, ownership, runtime, backend, cost, and recovery all agree before anyone presses go.
- [Why Coordination Guard Exists - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/coordination-guard-claims-into-policy): Coordination Guard was not born from a clean theory of Git as policy. It was born because four agents - politely, professionally, with great commit messages - kept staging, resetting, and cherry-picking through each other's claims, and the Saturday I lost untangling that mess was the Saturday I stopped trusting honor systems.
- [Evidence That Survives Multiple Machines - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/evidence-that-survives-machines): A note only your laptop can verify is half a record - and "trust me, it was on the other machine" is the worst sentence in incident response. The v2 Merkle forest, the KMS witness, and the mutable-signal ledger let a teammate or a CI runner verify the same evidence in 700 bytes, without your laptop in the room.
- [Cold Start Without Surprise Launches - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/fleet-designer-cold-start): The first time you run a fleet should not also be the first time it tells you a credential is missing, the daemon is on the wrong checkout, or the planned spend is roughly your rent. Cold start is supposed to read the repo, list what is missing, simulate the run, and let the human decide whether the bill is worth it.
- [Passkey Identity Across Machines - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/passkey-identity-across-machines): Single-node was the right answer for one laptop and exactly one human. Then the laptops multiplied, the phone showed up, and the recovery story collapsed into prayer. The Federated Sovereign is what replaces it: passkeys at the front, an abstract KMS in the middle, mobile-as-viewer at the edge, and a recovery flow you can actually run on a Tuesday.
- [PD Tube Turns UI Events Into Agent Work - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/pd-tube-event-reply-loop): PD Tube is a phone line. The browser button, the failing test, the editor lightbulb, the inbound webhook - they all dial the same number, and the agent already sitting in your repo picks up. No SDK, no MCP server, no hosted callback. Just a local socket and a threaded reply.
- [One Send, Every Listener: pd tube Goes Multi-Subscriber - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/pd-tube-multi-subscriber): I built a two-pane demo of pd tube — a human and a live agent talking over one channel. It worked. Then I added a third listener and the bug fell out of the sky: whichever terminal polled first swallowed the message and the rest saw an empty channel. A 'broadcast' channel was quietly behaving like a vending machine. Here's the shared-cursor race that caused it, the per-listener-cursor fix that turned it into real fan-out, and the regression test that documents the old bug on purpose. Shipped in v3.16.2.
- [Keeping the Map Honest - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/recovery-roadmap-map-truth): The roadmap says one thing, the recovery doc says another, the session notes say a third, and the live daemon is somehow doing a fourth. The fix is not more documents. It is one surface that reconciles all four into a map an operator can read in twenty seconds.
- [Red and White Stay In Their Lanes - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/red-and-white-stay-in-their-lanes): Two AI fleets argue about my whitepaper every month, and they are not allowed to talk to each other. One tries to break the paper; one tries to defend it. Here is the crypto that keeps them in their lanes, the three gates each round has to clear, and what shows up on the operator screen when somebody cheats.
- [Running Is Not the Same as Current - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/running-is-not-current): A daemon can be alive, reachable, answering on the right port, and still serving the version of itself you wrote three weeks ago. "Running" is a heartbeat. "Current" is a different question. Runtime provenance is what makes the second one answerable before you trust anything the UI or the CLI says.
- [Telemetry Is a Launch Gate - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/telemetry-is-a-launch-gate): A launch button that does not know what the run will cost is a slot machine in a nice typeface. The fix is unromantic: refuse to launch unless the backend can name the exact tokens, the exact rates, and the exact nonzero cost it has already written down.
- [The CLI Is For The Robots - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/the-cli-is-for-the-robots): I edited an .env.local file today. Wrong one. Three directories away from the one the daemon actually reads. The fleet sat there 401'ing for an hour while I edited the wrong file and felt productive. That is a product failure, not a user error. The operator does not run `pd` commands; the operator gets buttons. Here is the rule, the two feedback drops that came out of the incident, and what stays in the CLI.
- [Your Coding Agent Has Your Push Token - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/the-macaroon-gate): You hand an agent your repo and it has the real push token — nothing structural stops it pinning main at 3am. A stern wrapper does not help; if the agent holds the capability, the restraint is advice. The fix is a macaroon: a credential the agent can narrow but never widen, whose push is gated on a daemon-issued discharge that only exists while coordination rent is paid. And we did not assert it was sound — ProVerif checked it, found the attack the request-binding stops, and proved the gate holds against an active attacker.
- [The PR That Reviews Itself - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/the-pr-that-reviews-itself): You push at eleven at night. The CI gear-wheel is the only critic in the room. What if every PR you opened arrived with the adversarial review you would have asked for — six paid critics on the same git push you were already doing? The GitHub fleet, the bug it caught (14 green tests against a count that was structurally always 0), and what stays in your hands.
- [Your AI Subscription Already Powers A Fleet - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/blog/your-ai-subscription-powers-the-fleet): I'm in Claude Code or Codex about ten hours a day. The subscription isn't idle — but a person can only hold one cursor at a time, and the other streams (worktrees, midnight agents, post-commit hooks) are free to share the same hourly budget. The killer experience isn't 'saves money.' It's waking up to a feature that wasn't there last night. Here's the math, the rate-limit contention honesty, and where `pd nightshift` is going.

## White Papers

- [The Harbor Library - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/library): The seven-paper Harbor Library, read as one volume: four chapters explain local-first agent coordination, identity, and the harbor economy; three prove it with machine-checked formal verification.
- [Manifesto - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/manifesto): Software learned to hire its own help. Why a fleet of agents needs a harbor-master before anything else, how legibility becomes the product, and the seven papers that work it out.
- [Cryptography - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/security): What stops an agent you never authorized from touching your code — and the proofs behind it. Capability attenuation, signed envelopes, collateralized work, and Ostrom-style commons governance, with the Anchor Protocol verified in ProVerif.
- [Whitepaper - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper): Read the technical whitepaper behind Port Daddy: local-first agent coordination, signed identity, capability boundaries, sessions, and recoverable work.
- [The Anchor Protocol - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/anchor-protocol): A guided read of the Anchor Protocol paper — what an "identity for a process" should even mean, how to mint one out of off-the-shelf cryptography, and why a problem that felt unsolvable in 2010 is now a long weekend's work.
- [The Bonded Commons - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/bonded-commons): A guided read of the Bonded Commons paper: why mutual visibility beats locks once you have more than a handful of agents, what kind of refundable "deposit" makes that visibility honest instead of theatrical, and how a tiny insurance market beats any single human picking the deposit size by hand.
- [The Federated Harbor - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/federated-harbor): A guided read of the Federated Harbor paper — why two trustworthy local daemons can still fail jointly, what four small primitives close the gap, and the honest list of open questions the paper does not answer.
- [The Harbor Economy - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/harbor-economy): A guided read of the market chapter: the three-sided market and its one conserving ledger, the cross-harbor transfer ceremony and federation, and the honest reconciliations — the cohomology of double-spend, the lax functor of conservation, and the Myerson–Satterthwaite tax on any honest market.
- [The Legible Swarm - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/legible-swarm): A guided read of the volume’s flagship: legibility-with-zoom as the product a solo developer pays for today, the read-poverty bottleneck that decides the next order of magnitude, and an attention queue spined on Signal Detection Theory rather than raw throughput.
- [The Single-Writer Kernel - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/single-writer-kernel): A guided read of the substrate chapter: why a single writer beats consensus on one machine, the kernel’s invariants stated as theorems, and a careful split of durability by fault class — survives a process crash, does not promise to survive a power cut.
- [From Spawn to Person - Port Daddy](https://portdaddy.dev/whitepaper/spawn-to-person): A guided read of the bridge chapter: the role-vs-person distinction made load-bearing, why reputation is not a bandit problem, a multi-dimensional reputation scored by neutral conflict-free judges, and the honest naming of cross-operator attestation as the unbuilt keystone.
